title: Should top managers be promoted from within the company, or hired from outside?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The difference between companies is people. With capital and technology in plentiful supply, the critical resource for companies in the knowledge era will be human talent. Companies full of ‘star’ achievers will, by definition, outperform organisations without them. So firms should compete for the most talented people, attract them from other companies, pay them very well, and get rid of second-raters. This in essence has been the recruitment strategy of the ambitious companies of the past decade, given definitive form by the consultancy McKinsey in the book The War for Talent. Although the intensity of the warfare subsequently subsided, it has been warming up again as the economy tightens: labour shortages, for example, are the reason that many governments are welcoming workers from abroad.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The diagnosis – people are important – is so obvious it scarcely needs saying, but the apparently logical prescription – hire the best – is, like so much in management, profoundly wrong. The point was illuminated by the collapse of the major American company Enron, whose leaders, as a New Yorker article called ‘The Talent Myth’ related, were so convinced of their own cleverness that they believed that collective intelligence is the sum of a lot of individual intelligences. In fact, in a profound sense the two are opposites. Enron believed in stars, noted author Malcolm Gladwell, because they didn't believe in systems. But companies don't just create; they execute and compete and co-ordinate the efforts of many people, and the organisations that are most successful at that task are the ones where the ‘system is the star’.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The truth is that a company can't win the talent war by hiring stars – only lose it. New light is thrown on why this should be so by a study of the careers of 1,000 top analysts, published in the Harvard Business Review. The researchers found that when a company recruited a star performer, three things happened.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: First, star quality didn't easily transfer from one organisation to another. In many cases, when star performers switched employers, their performance dropped sharply and in some instances never recovered. Few people realise how much success is due to the working environment – systems, processes, leadership, accumulated embedded learning, which are absent in and can't be transported to the new firm. Moreover, precisely because of their past success, stars were unwilling to learn new tricks and antagonised those (on whom they now unknowingly depended) who could teach them. So they left, increasing their salary as they did so – a surprisingly high 36 per cent moved on within three years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Secondly, the performance of their new team suffered as a result of the tensions and resentment created by their arrival. Hiring a star has been compared to an organ transplant. The new organ can damage others by taking most of the blood supply, other organs can start aching or threaten to stop working, or the body can reject the transplant altogether.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Thirdly, the share price fell, as investors sold stock, evidently to punish the company for its extravagance in spending money on the expensive new appointee. This is ironic, since the motive for importing stars was often to improve the share price.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Everyone accepts the cliché that people make the organisation – but, in fact, to a far greater extent, the organisation makes the people. This is as true in the world of football as in business. Some football clubs buy very good – and very expensive – players, but the team may be less than the sum of its parts. Others put much more emphasis on developing systems: a setting within which less good players can improve, and which helps everyone to form an effective team. These clubs are often more successful than those with the stars. Similarly, a study of the performance of fund managers showed that just 30 per cent of variation in fund performance was due to the individual, compared to 70 per cent to the company-specific setting.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: That will be no surprise to those familiar with systems thinking. Deming, the management thinker, used to say that there was no point in criticising people when 90 per cent of performance variation was down to the system within which they worked. Consistent improvement, he said, is a matter not of raising the level of individual intelligence, but of the learning of the organisation as a whole.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: So if not by hiring stars, how can a company compete in the war for talent? It should grow its own. Some companies are not only better at creating stars, but also at retaining them. Because they have a much more sophisticated view of the interdependent relationship between star and system, they keep them longer without needing to pay exorbitant salaries. The star system is glamorous – for the few. But companies that use it rarely benefit to the extent that they expect. Bringing in high-paid talent from outside is rarely worthwhile, and the impact can be dire.

groups.title: Research published in the Harvard Business Review
content: Research into the working lives of a large number of successful people working as {{19}} revealed that hiring stars had three common effects. The stars often failed to maintain their performance, as much of their success came from the factors making up their old company’s {{20}}. In fact, many of them soon left their new company to join another firm at a higher {{21}}. Secondly, there was often a negative effect on co-workers in their {{22}} at the new company. Thirdly, investors reduced their commitment to the company.
